title: An issue's own named blocker closed, and the issue is still open
author: off-by-one
description: Compares open issues against the repository's own issue set: an issue's body names itself 'blocked by #N' (or 'blocked on #N'), and #N has since closed, but the blocked issue itself was never revisited -- no comment, no state change, nothing. Unlike a 'duplicate of #N' marker (duplicate-issue-still-open), which claims equivalence and implies the duplicate should close too, a blocker marker claims only a dependency -- once #N closes, the blocked issue's own work becomes actionable again, and GitHub gives that transition no auto-anything either: no auto-close, no auto-comment, no flag anywhere in the API. A dependency, unlike a duplicate, is never expected to close on its own, so this recipe's gap is narrower and more honest than 'this should be closed': it surfaces only the fact that the named blocker resolved, and nothing on either record shows anyone came back to look.
confidence_notes: Age-gated on how long the named blocker has been closed while the blocked issue sits open, not flat. Under 24 hours since the blocker closed scores 0.5 (below the 0.70 bar, weighed in the tail not hidden -- a human may not have circled back within a day of the blocker resolving). At or past 24 hours it scores a flat 0.85 -- an unambiguous, non-fuzzy signal, a blocker marker naming an issue number that already reads closed. The 24h window matches duplicate-issue-still-open's and overdue-milestone-still-open's own bar (a clear, easily-verified resolution signal deserves a short grace window, not a long one), reused here rather than inventing a new number for a structurally similar self-declared-prose-marker family. An issue naming no blocker marker, naming a blocker that is still open, or naming a blocker that does not exist at all is excluded at confidence 0.0, named not hidden -- the identical discipline every recipe before this one holds. An issue that is already closed itself carries no gap left to surface, whatever its body once claimed.
